summary: Delivered on the first day of Kartik at the Krishna-Balaram Mandir in Vrindavan, this lecture first glorifies the month of Kartik, also called Damodara, which Indradyumna Swami explains bears this name both because Damodara is the worshipable deity of the year's final month and because it commemorates Mother Yashoda binding baby Krishna to the grinding mortar with a rope (dama = rope, udara = belly); he adds that Krishna was also bound by Radharani's golden belt. He establishes Radharani as 'Kartika Devi,' the presiding goddess of the month, citing Rupa Goswami, Raghunatha dasa Goswami and Sanatana Goswami, and notes that the Brahma-vaivarta Purana enjoins that Radha must be adored on this first full-moon day. The heart of the class narrates the Saradiya (autumn) Rasa Lila, which occurred at midnight on this very day 5,000 years ago and is celebrated again tonight; he first defends the propriety of hearing rasa-lila for sincere sadhakas from authorized sources, quoting Bhagavatam 10.33.39 and Chaitanya-charitamrita that such faithful hearing conquers lust, the disease of the heart. Following Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura's Sarartha-darshini commentary, he recounts how the gopis, maddened in separation after Krishna leaves the dance with Radha, imitate and enact his pastimes (including demons, whose roles Yogamaya/Purnamasi assumes per Kavikarnapura), then discover Krishna's footprints marked with a flag, lotus, thunderbolt, elephant goad and barley corn beside Radha's smaller prints. He describes how the different groups of gopis (Vipaksha, Tatastha, Suhrit-paksha) react, quotes the famous verse glorifying the gopi who 'worshipped best' (aradhana, the root of the name Radha, per CC Adi 4.87), and explains that Radha asked Krishna to carry her not out of pride but out of compassion for her friends, after which Krishna vanished, the gopis found the fainted Radharani, revived her, and sang the Gopi-gita on the bank of the Yamuna. Throughout he ties the pastime to the purpose of Parikrama, wandering Vrindavan 'in search of Krishna' in the footsteps of the Goswamis, and to taking vratas during Kartik, illustrating with stories such as Prabhupada telling a Western disciple to 'just wander,' the Polish festival drama where a little girl cried out 'Mommy, I want Krishna,' and Prabhupada's teaching that the Hare Krishna mantra means 'my friend, my friend, my friend.' He closes by reassuring devotees anxious about that night's inauspicious lunar eclipse that worshiping Radharani, the source of all auspiciousness, removes all danger, and mentions the tradition of offering a big pot of sweet rice on the rooftop for Radha-Krishna and the gopis.
key_points: Kartik is the month of Damodara, named both because Damodara is the worshipable deity of the year's final month and because Mother Yashoda bound baby Krishna to the mortar with a rope (dama) around his belly (udara); it is supremely auspicious for spiritual practice, one Kartik morning bath equaling bathing in all holy places.

Radharani is glorified as Kartika Devi and Vrindavaneshwari, the presiding goddess of the month; scripture enjoins that she must be adored on Kartik's first full-moon day, and worship performed for her pleasure is blessed by her.

Hearing the rasa-lila from an authorized spiritual authority is not forbidden but beneficial for aspiring devotees, since faithful hearing conquers lust and nullifies the disease of the heart (Bhagavatam 10.33.39; CC Antya 5).

Following Vishvanatha Chakravarti's Sarartha-darshini, the Saradiya Rasa Lila unfolds in phases: after Krishna leaves the dance with Radha, the gopis go mad in separation (pramada, vipralambha-bhava), console themselves by imitating and dramatizing his pastimes, then track his marked footprints alongside Radha's.

Radharani is the topmost lover possessing mahabhava; Krishna leaves the dance with her, then abandons even her, so that her unrivaled love may be revealed; her name derives from aradhana, 'she who worships Krishna best,' and Radha asked to be carried out of compassion for her friends, not pride.

In shared separation from Krishna, even rival gopis' feelings of rivalry transform into mutual affection, and they unite to revive the fainted Radharani; Prabhupada applied this principle to devotees cooperating in ISKCON despite being culturally many but spiritually one.

Parikrama means wandering Vrindavan in search of Krishna in the footsteps of the Goswamis (e.g., Sanatana Goswami circumambulating Govardhana daily); devotees should take vratas during Kartik (extra japa, more reading, less sleep, avoiding mundane news), and the night's inauspicious lunar eclipse holds no danger for those worshiping Radharani, the source of all auspiciousness.
references: Krishna Book, ch. 29 (Prabhupada's summary of the setting of the rasa dance, quoted as the opening) - the rising full moon, cool festive atmosphere, and Krishna's flute enchanting the gopis.

Adi-varaha Purana (Varaha Purana) - the verse that the very sight of Vrindavan destroys all sins in the heart ('As sunrise destroys the dark of night...'); linked to Lord Varaha glorifying Vrindavan to Bhumi at Vishram-ghat after slaying Hiranyaksha.
Padma Purana - one who renders devotional service in Vrindavan, especially in Kartik, ends up hankering only for pure devotional service.
Hari-bhakti-vilasa 16.166 - one who even as a joke worships Krishna in Mathura during Kartik attains the Lord's supreme abode.
Hari-bhakti-vilasa 16.197 (Sanatana Goswami) - Lord Damodara is very pleased if during Kartik one worships Radharani's deity for her pleasure.

Krishna-karnamrita (Bilvamangala Thakura), verse 110, with Krishnadasa Kaviraja Goswami's commentary - Krishna, having missed a rendezvous, was bound by Radha's golden belt and became known as Damodara.
Damodarashtaka by Satyavrata Muni - obeisances to the rope that bound Krishna's abdomen and to his beloved Srimati Radharani.
Stavamala by Rupa Goswami - describes Vrindavaneshwari Srimati Radharani as Kartika Devi, the goddess of Kartika.
Radhika-ashtottara-shata-nama-stotram by Raghunatha dasa Goswami - Radha is Damodara's unrivaled beloved who bestows auspiciousness during Kartik.
Nectar of Devotion (Prabhupada's study of Rupa Goswami's Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu) - one should surrender to Krishna in all respects and observe particular vows during the auspicious month of Kartik.
Brahma-vaivarta Purana, Prakriti Khanda, ch. 34, verses 90-91 - on the first day of Kartik during the full moon, Radha the beloved of Krishna must be adored.
Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu (cited as 2.1.209) quoting the Brihad-vamana Purana - Krishna states that of all his enchanting pastimes, the rasa-lila so overwhelms his heart that he cannot describe it.

Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.33.39 - one who faithfully hears or describes the Lord's affairs with the gopis attains pure devotional service and quickly becomes sober, conquering lust, the disease of the heart.

Chaitanya-charitamrita, Antya-lila 5.45-47 (with Prabhupada's purport quoting Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura) - hearing the rasa dance with faith immediately nullifies lusty desires and the agitation of the three modes.

Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.31 with Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura's Sarartha-darshini commentary - the phased analysis of the Saradiya Rasa Lila (gopis' madness, imitation, following footprints, Radha's supremacy).
Siksastakam (verse 7, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu) - 'O Govinda, feeling your separation I consider a moment to be like twelve years... I feel all vacant in the world in your absence.'
Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.30.25 - the gopis come upon Krishna's footprints marked with flag, lotus, thunderbolt, elephant goad and barley corn, beside Radha's smaller prints.
Ananda-vrindavana-champu by Kavikarnapura - Yogamaya (Purnamasi), not the gopis, assumes the demon roles; and Radha asks to be carried out of compassion for her friends rather than from pride.

Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.30.28 (the 'anayaradhito' verse) - 'Certainly this gopi perfectly worshipped Govinda, since he abandoned the rest of us and brought her to a secluded place' (quoted as the famous verse glorifying Radha).
Chaitanya-charitamrita, Adi-lila 4.87 - her worship (aradhana) consists of fulfilling Krishna's desires; therefore the Puranas call her Radhika (the source of the name Radha).
Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.30.37 - the special gopi, feeling proud, tells Keshava she can walk no further and asks to be carried.
Sarartha-darshini on Bhagavatam 10.30.40 (an unnamed author quoted by Vishvanatha Chakravarti) - 'Separation from a mutual beloved awakens the spontaneous display of heartfelt affection in lovers.'
Sarartha-darshini on Bhagavatam 10.32 - a gopi suggests the forest is so dark that even moonlight cannot enter, so better to return to the Yamuna and let Krishna come to them.
Gopi-gita (Srimad-Bhagavatam, ch. 31) - the gopis sing in a unified concert of voices on the bank of the Yamuna, which draws Krishna back.
Radha-kripa-kataksha-stava-raja (concluding verse) - 'O goddess whose face eclipses millions of autumn moons in an auspicious way... when will you cast your merciful sidelong glance upon me?'
stories: Damodara bound to the mortar — Mother Yashoda ties baby Krishna's belly with a rope to the grinding mortar, giving the month its name (dama = rope, udara = belly).
Bound by Radha's golden belt — having missed a rendezvous, Krishna is frowned upon by Radha and bound with her golden belt, again becoming 'Damodara.'
The gopis imitate Krishna — maddened in separation, the gopis dramatize his pastimes; Yogamaya (Purnamasi), not the gopis, assumes the demon roles of Putana and Trinavarta.
Krishna's marked footprints — the gopis find his prints stamped with flag, lotus, thunderbolt, elephant goad and barley corn, beside Radha's smaller prints, and know he took her.
Radha asks to be carried — not from pride but from compassion, she feigns fatigue so Krishna will move off and her friends can reach her; he then vanishes 'as if Rahu had devoured the full moon.'
Reviving the fainted Radha — even rival gopis unite to comfort her, and the lingering fragrance of Krishna on their bodies rouses her.
The Gopi-gita on the Yamuna — in a unified concert of voices the gopis sing their hearts out, drawing Krishna back.
'Just wander' — a Western devotee asks Prabhupada what to do in Vrindavan, and Prabhupada simply says to wander the lila-sthanas and imbibe their moods.
'Mommy, I want Krishna' — after the Damodara drama on the Polish festival tour, a six-year-old girl stands on her mother's lap and cries out, making 35 years of struggle worthwhile.
quotes: It means my friend, my friend, my friend.
